2. Study Context and Background
2.1 Research Problem
Climate variability — including low precipitation, flooding, high temperatures, prolonged sunshine, and delayed
rainfall — threatens agricultural productivity, leading to food insecurity and chronic poverty, especially among
resource-constrained smallholder farmers. Rain-fed agriculture, which dominates small-scale farming in Africa, is
particularly susceptible. The study tests the hypothesis that adopting Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) is a
significant strategy for climate change adaptation.

  Kenya is vulnerable to climate change and has implemented multiple national frameworks.

3. Climate-Smart Agriculture: Definition and Practices
3.1 Definition of CSA
CSA is defined as methods, management strategies, and technical developments that sustainably increase
productivity, improve resilience, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and better achieve food security and
development objectives (Chandra et al. 2018). It is based on a 'triple-win' impact: increasing production, improving
resilience, and lowering emissions. Farm-level CSA techniques are described as deliberate agricultural adaptation
or environmental management methods applied on plots owned, leased, or used by a household.

Null hypothesis (H0): Adopting CSA is not a significant strategy for climate change adaptation. Alternative

5.2 Explanation of Adoption Patterns
High adoption – Synthetic fertilizers (95%)
  Release nutrients quickly and produce high yields to meet food demand.
 Can be applied instantly; organic fertilizers require time to decompose and are bulky.
High adoption – Crop rotation, agroforestry, intercropping, rainwater harvesting (>80%)
  Ensure differential nutrient uptake; improve soil fertility; reduce chemical fertilizer needs.
 Agroforestry improves land productivity, provides hospitable microclimate, carbon content.
 Water harvesting increases yields (Parrott & Marsden 2002 cited Senegal millet/peanut example).
Low adoption – Potato mini-tubers (1.7%) and apical rooted cuttings (7.5%)
  Lack of technical know-how among farmers.
 High cost of purchasing seedlings.
 Inability to reinvent (replicate) these practices independently.
 Require additional investment and higher recurring costs compared to other CSA practices.
 Management gap and technological gap are the two contributors to the productivity disparity.

8. Detailed Analysis: Four Significant CSA Potentials
8.1 Reducing Soil Erosion (Odds Ratio = 7.286, p = 0.001)
CSA reduces soil erosion among adopters 7.286 times more than non-adopters.

Mechanisms:
  Low/no-till farming leaves agricultural residues on the field after harvest, acting as protective cover.
 Cover crops planted during fallow periods stabilise soil with roots and add organic matter.
 Agroforestry — trees and shrubs create natural windbreaks, slowing wind and preventing erosion.
 Terracing and contour ploughing on sloping land minimise erosive power of water runoff.
 Soil health practices (organic matter addition, fertiliser management, reducing soil compaction) minimise
erosion.
 USDA (2021): perennial cover crops in strip systems increase soil carbon sequestration, build soil health,
reduce erosion.
Caution:
  Reforestation/afforestation in sensitive ecosystems or steep slopes may paradoxically worsen soil erosion if
implemented incautiously.
8.2 Increasing Livelihood Diversification (Odds Ratio = 10.706, p < 0.001)
CSA increases livelihood diversification among adopters 10.706 times more than non-adopters. This is the
strongest effect among the four significant potentials.
Mechanisms:
  Crop diversification improves farmer and landscape resilience.
 Commercialisation and enhanced farm profitability enable smallholders to expand and scale.
 Surplus income from CSA-driven higher yields can fund off-farm businesses (agri-processing, service-based
ventures).
 Agroforestry and sustainable forest management provide timber, fuelwood, fruits, nuts, and forest products.
 Eco-tourism and nature-based business opportunities created through environmentally sound CSA
behaviours.
 Community-based projects (cooperatives, community gardens, market linkages) open shared livelihood
prospects.
Limitation:
  Non-agricultural livelihood transformation may merely be a poor coping strategy if smallholders lack access to
financial resources, land, water, and technology required to diversify.
8.3 Reducing Input Expenses (Odds Ratio = 6.000, p = 0.002)
CSA reduces input expenses among adopters 6.0 times more than non-adopters.
Mechanisms:
  Composting and crop residues as mulch or green manure reduce demand for chemical fertilisers.
 Integrated Pest Management (IPM) reduces reliance on chemical pesticides.
 Contour ploughing and agroforestry prevent soil erosion and water loss, reducing recovery costs after drought
or flood.
 CSA enables access to premium markets that reward sustainable practices (certifications, labelling), helping
cover input costs.
 Mulching and no-till farming reduce labour-intensive weeding and ploughing, reducing labour costs.

 Khatri-Chhetri et al. (2016) found smallholder farmers significantly benefited financially from CSA.
Caveat:
  Early adopters face yield risk, equipment costs, and input costs as initial barriers.
 Monast and Yeoman (2023) note early adopters may be shut out of ecosystem markets due to extra
requirements.
8.4 Increasing Product Quality (Odds Ratio = 6.182, p = 0.003)
CSA increases product quality among adopters 6.182 times more than non-adopters.
Mechanisms:
  Organic management practices improve biotic elements of soil health (microbial activity and diversity),
improving crop quality.
 Balanced nutrient management (soil testing, precision inputs) ensures crops receive adequate nutrients —
improves nutritional value.
 Rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation ensure adequate water supply without waterlogging — tastier, more
flavorful produce.
 Appropriate post-harvest handling (storage, transportation) maintains produce in better shape.
 Climate-smart certifications and traceability systems boost consumer confidence and product perception.
 'Climate-smart' labelled products may command higher prices as consumer awareness of sustainability
grows.
 Reilly et al. (2013): organic fertiliser in onion fields resulted in soil-suppressive functional groups dominating
over pathogens.
 Reganold et al. (2010): CSA measures on strawberry farms (organic amendments) resulted in higher-quality
fruit.
Limitation:
  Extreme weather events (prolonged droughts, floods) can still affect crop quality despite CSA adoption.
 Limited access to inputs (quality seeds, fertilisers, equipment) can hinder product quality improvement in
some regions.

10. Conclusions and Recommendations
10.1 Key Conclusions
  Average of 64.56% of smallholder potato farmers in Gilgil Sub-County adopted CSA practices.
 Synthetic fertilisers were the most adopted CSA (95%); mini-tubers were the least adopted (1.7%).
 Binary regression confirmed: CSA is a statistically significant climate change adaptation strategy (Wald
chi-squared = 49.417, df = 1, p < 0.001).
 Implementing CSA increases farmers' chances of adapting to climate change by 19 times compared to
non-adopters.
 CSA significantly contributes to adaptation through four pathways: reducing soil erosion, increasing livelihood
diversification, reducing input expenses, and increasing product quality.
 These four benefits create a ripple of positive impacts: preserved soil fertility, spread income risk, sustainable
farming motivation, and reduced waste along the supply chain.
10.2 Recommendations
 Recommendation
Rationale
Use experiential learning approaches
Allows farmers to actively engage with new CSA practices and technologies, leading to better understanding and adoption
Establish linkages between research institutions and farmers
Facilitates exchange of information/expertise; creates dynamic feedback loop that fosters CSA acceptance
Capitalise on progressive farmers as role models
Progressive farmers can share experiences, demonstrate CSA benefits, and provide practical guidance to fellow farmers
Address barriers to potato mini-tubers and apical cuttings adoption
Technical know-how, cost support, and reinvention capacity needed to close the technological and management gaps
Promote CSA through government extension and NGO partnerships
SNV, CaWSA-C, CARP+, and government extension officers model effective delivery channels
11. Glossary of Key Terms
Term
Definition
CSA – Climate-Smart Agriculture
Methods, management strategies, and technical developments that sustainably increase productivity, improve resilience, lower GHG emissions, and achieve food security. FAO concept first used in 2009.
Triple-win
The three core CSA objectives: (1) increase production/food security, (2) improve resilience/adaptation, (3) reduce GHG emissions/mitigation.

Term
Definition
KCSAS
Kenya Climate-Smart Agriculture Strategy (2017–2026). Guides changes to agricultural systems through integrated approach.
NCCAP
National Climate Change Action Plan (Kenya, 2013–2017). Part of Kenya's climate governance framework.
NCCRS
National Climate Change Response Strategy (Kenya, 2010).
CaWSA-C
Climate and Water Smart Agriculture Centre. Active in Gilgil Sub-County.
CARP+
Community Action Research Project. Active in Gilgil Sub-County.
RUFORUM
Regional Universities Forum for Capacity Building in Agriculture. Provided funding through MasterCard Foundation.
NACOSTI
National Commission for Science, Technology, and Innovation (Kenya). Issued ethics approval.
Binary logistic regression
Statistical method used to predict a binary outcome (adapts/does not adapt) from predictor variables. Results expressed as odds ratios (Exp B).
Odds ratio / Exp(B)
How many times more likely CSA adopters are to experience a given outcome compared to non-adopters. E.g., Exp(B) = 7.286 means 7.3x more likely.
Wald statistic
Test statistic in logistic regression used to assess whether a predictor is statistically significant.
IPM – Integrated Pest Management
Approach combining biological control, crop rotation, prudent pesticide use to manage pests with minimal environmental impact.
Apical rooted cuttings
Potato seedlings produced through tissue culture; disease-free seed material. Classified as a CSA practice in this study.
Mini-tubers
Small potato seed tubers produced through modern seed technology. Classified as a CSA practice.
Agroforestry
Integration of trees and shrubs into agricultural landscapes; improves soil fertility, provides windbreaks, diversifies income.
Smallholder farmer
Farmer operating on a small area of land, often with limited capital, relying on family labour and facing significant resource constraints.
Agro-ecological zone
Classification of land areas by climate, soil, and vegetation to guide agricultural recommendations. Gilgil is in Zone III of Kenya.
Cronbach Alpha
Measure of questionnaire reliability. Score of 0.805 obtained (threshold for reliability: >0.70).
Coefficient of variation (C)
Statistical measure of relative variability used in Nassiuma sample size formula. Set at 21% in this study.
